A **reduction formula** is wanted, and it comes from integrating by parts with the
"invisible" factor 1.
**Step 1 — set up the integration by parts.**
Iₙ = ∫(log x)ⁿ dx = ∫(log x)ⁿ **· 1** dx
Take u = (log x)ⁿ and dv = dx, so that
du = n(log x)^(n−1) · (1/x) dx and v = x
**Step 2 — apply ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du.**
Iₙ = x(log x)ⁿ − ∫ x · n(log x)^(n−1) · (1/x) dx
The x and the 1/x cancel:
Iₙ = x(log x)ⁿ − n∫(log x)^(n−1) dx
**Step 3 — recognise the remaining integral.** By the definition of Iₙ with n replaced by
n − 1,
∫(log x)^(n−1) dx = **I_(n−1)**
so
**Iₙ = x(log x)ⁿ − n I_(n−1)**
**Step 4 — rearrange into the form asked for.**
**Iₙ + n I_(n−1) = x(log x)ⁿ** ✓
**Check with n = 1.**
I₁ = ∫log x dx = **x log x − x** (the standard result)
I₀ = ∫(log x)⁰ dx = ∫1 dx = **x**
Then I₁ + 1·I₀ = (x log x − x) + x = **x log x** = x(log x)¹ ✓
**Check with n = 2.**
I₂ = ∫(log x)²dx = x(log x)² − 2I₁ = x(log x)² − 2(x log x − x)
I₂ + 2I₁ = x(log x)² − 2I₁ + 2I₁ = **x(log x)²** ✓

I₃ = x(log x)³ − 3I₂, I₂ = x(log x)² − 2I₁, I₁ = x log x − I₀, I₀ = x
so no integral of this family ever needs to be attacked from scratch.

integral; the essential content of the answer is **x(log x)ⁿ**.
**The distractors** — (log x)ⁿ/n and (log x)^(n+1)/(n + 1) — are what would come from
treating log x as if it were a plain variable and applying the power rule, forgetting that
d(log x)/dx = 1/x rather than 1.
∴ x(log x)ⁿ + c.

The constant term **e** of a polynomial is its value at **x = 0**, so there is no need to
expand the determinant in general — only to evaluate it at a single point.
**Step 1 — see why.** Writing f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + cx² + dx + e and putting x = 0, every
term with a factor of x vanishes:
**f(0) = e**
So e is simply the determinant evaluated at x = 0.
**Step 2 — substitute x = 0 into each entry** of
| x³ + 3x   x − 1   x + 3 |
| x + 1     −2x     x − 4 |
| x − 3     x + 4   3x    |
giving
| 0    −1    3 |
| 1     0   −4 |
| −3    4    0 |
**Step 3 — expand along the first row.**
= 0 × [(0)(0) − (−4)(4)] − (−1) × [(1)(0) − (−4)(−3)] + 3 × [(1)(4) − (0)(−3)]
**first term:** 0 × (0 + 16) = **0**
**second term:** +1 × (0 − 12) = **−12**
**third term:** 3 × (4 − 0) = **+12**
**Step 4 — add.**
e = 0 − 12 + 12 = **0** ✓
**A structural check.** Notice that the matrix at x = 0 is **skew-symmetric**: its transpose
is its negative, since the (i, j) entry is minus the (j, i) entry throughout and the
diagonal is all zeros. For any skew-symmetric matrix of **odd** order,
|Aᵀ| = |A| and |−A| = (−1)³|A| = −|A|
so |A| = −|A|, forcing **|A| = 0** ✓ The answer follows with no arithmetic at all — a
useful thing to spot, since every odd-order skew-symmetric determinant vanishes.
**Why not expand the whole determinant?** It would mean multiplying out a 3 × 3 of
polynomials, collecting five coefficients, and reading off only the last — a great deal of
work for one number. Substituting a single value is the standard trick for extracting a
particular coefficient: x = 0 gives the constant term, and the sum of all coefficients is
obtained from x = 1.
∴ 0.

expression.
**Step 1 — sum the series.** The series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ⋯ is geometric with first term 1

**1/(1 − x)**

= e^(log[1/(1 − x)])

**King property** of definite integrals does all the work.
**Step 1 — reduce to the quarter-circle.** The integrand
F(x) = cos⁴x/(cos⁴x + sin⁴x)
satisfies F(π − x) = F(x), because cos(π − x) = −cos x and sin(π − x) = sin x, and both are
raised to the **even** power 4 so the signs disappear. A function symmetric about x = π/2
contributes equally on each half, so
I = ∫₀^π F(x)dx = **2∫₀^(π/2) F(x)dx**
Call the half-integral J.
**Step 2 — apply the King property to J.** For any a,
∫₀^a f(x)dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x)dx
With a = π/2, using cos(π/2 − x) = sin x and sin(π/2 − x) = cos x:
J = ∫₀^(π/2) cos⁴x/(cos⁴x + sin⁴x) dx = ∫₀^(π/2) **sin⁴x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x)** dx
The denominator is unchanged — it is symmetric in sine and cosine — while the numerator has
swapped.
**Step 3 — add the two expressions for J.**
2J = ∫₀^(π/2) [cos⁴x + sin⁴x]/(cos⁴x + sin⁴x) dx
= ∫₀^(π/2) **1** dx
= **π/2**
so **J = π/4**

finding, yet the definite integral is exact. That is the point of the King property: it
turns an impossible integration into a trivial addition.
**A sanity check by symmetry.** Over [0, π/2] the functions cos⁴x and sin⁴x are mirror

The upper limit here is **π**, so the result must be doubled — reading the limits carefully
is half the question.

there is a standard result for exactly this situation.
**Step 1 — state the property.** If f(a + b − x) = f(x) on [a, b], then
**∫ₐᵇ x f(x) dx = [(a + b)/2] ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx**
**Step 2 — prove it**, since the proof is short and makes the result memorable. Let
I = ∫ₐᵇ x f(x)dx. By the King property, replacing x with a + b − x:
I = ∫ₐᵇ (a + b − x) f(a + b − x) dx
= ∫ₐᵇ (a + b − x) f(x) dx (using the given symmetry)
= (a + b)∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx − ∫ₐᵇ x f(x) dx
= (a + b)∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx − I
Therefore **2I = (a + b)∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx**, which is the result ✓
**Step 3 — identify a and b.** The symmetry is about π + e − x, so a + b = **π + e**, and
the integral runs from **a = e** to **b = π** ✓ consistent, since e + π = π + e.
**Step 4 — substitute the given value.** With ∫ₑ^π f(x)dx = 2/(e + π):
∫ₑ^π x f(x)dx = [(π + e)/2] × 2/(e + π)
= (π + e)/(e + π)
= **1** ✓
The (π + e) cancels completely, which is why the answer is the clean number 1 — the
question was built so that it would.
**What the symmetry means geometrically.** The midpoint of [e, π] is (e + π)/2, and the
condition says the graph of f is a mirror image about the vertical line through it.
Weighting by x then has the same effect as weighting everything by the midpoint value,
which is precisely what the formula states.

holds, so ∫₀^π x sin x dx = (π/2)∫₀^π sin x dx = (π/2)(2) = **π** — a standard result that
the same property delivers in one line.

and integrate.
**Step 1 — divide by x** to make the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1:
x(dy/dx) + 2y = x²
**dy/dx + (2/x)y = x**
so **P = 2/x** and **Q = x**.
**Step 2 — find the integrating factor.**

**Step 3 — multiply the standard form through by x².**

integrating factor is for.
**Step 4 — integrate both sides.**
x²y = ∫x³ dx = **x⁴/4 + k**
**Step 5 — solve for y.**

Work outward from the inside: first the **contrapositive** of p → ~q, then the **converse**
of that.
**Step 1 — take the contrapositive of p → ~q.** It negates both parts and swaps them. With
A = p and B = ~q,
~B = ~(~q) = **q** and ~A = **~p**
so the contrapositive is
**q → ~p**
(the double negation on q collapsing to q is the step to watch.)
**Step 2 — take the converse of q → ~p**, which just swaps the two sides:
**~p → q** ✓
**A shortcut worth knowing.** Contrapositive followed by converse always yields the
**inverse**. The inverse of p → ~q negates both parts:
~p → ~(~q) = **~p → q** ✓ the same answer in one step.
**Checking the options.**
p → q ✗ — this negates nothing
~p → ~q ✗ — this would be the inverse if the original were p → q, but the original already
carries a ~q, so the second part becomes q, not ~q. This is the trap, and the commonest
wrong answer.
~q → p ✗ — a swap without the right negations
**~p → q** ✓
**Where the trap comes from.** Reading "inverse of p → ~q" and mechanically writing
"~p → ~q" forgets that the consequent is already negated. Negating ~q gives **q**. Writing
each double negation out in full, ~(~q) = q, is the discipline that prevents it.
**A concrete reading.** Let p be "it is raining" and q "the ground is dry", so p → ~q says
"if it is raining, the ground is not dry". Its contrapositive is "if the ground is dry, it
is not raining" — q → ~p ✓ and the converse of that is "if it is not raining, the ground is
dry" — ~p → q ✓ which is a different (and dubious) claim, as the inverse always is.
∴ ~p → q.

The **contrapositive** of p → q is **~q → ~p** — negate both parts **and** reverse them.
**Step 1 — name the parts.** "If x is a prime number, then x is odd" is p → q with
**p:** x is a prime number
**q:** x is odd
**Step 2 — form ~q → ~p.**
~q: x is **not odd**
~p: x is **not a prime number**
so the contrapositive reads
"If x is **not odd**, then x is **not a prime number**" ✓
**Step 3 — check the distractors.**
"If x is not a prime number, then x is not odd" is **~p → ~q**, the **inverse** ✗ — both
parts negated but **not** reversed, which is the single commonest error here.
"If x is a prime number, then x is not odd" is p → ~q ✗ — only the consequent negated.
"If x is not a prime number, then x is odd" is ~p → q ✗ — only the antecedent negated.
**The truth check.** The contrapositive always has the **same truth value** as the original,
and here both are false in the same way: 2 is prime but not odd, so the original fails;
and 2 is not odd yet **is** prime, so the contrapositive fails too — on the very same
counter-example ✓ That shared counter-example is itself evidence the two statements are
equivalent.
Contrast the **inverse**, "if x is not prime then x is not odd": its counter-example is
x = 9, which is not prime but is odd. A **different** counter-example, because it is a
different statement.
**Why the contrapositive matters.** Because it is logically equivalent, a theorem can be
proved by proving its contrapositive instead — often much easier. "If n² is even then n is
even" is awkward head-on, but its contrapositive, "if n is odd then n² is odd", follows in
one line from n = 2k + 1.
∴ If x is not odd, then x is not a prime number.
